question: For many years, forest firefighters have been waiting in vain for Directive 1999/70/EC to be transposed in Spain. Until it is transposed, 290 jobs hang in the balance, leaving our forests unprotected.

On 22 February 2024, the Court of Justice of the European Union ruled that the concept of a ‘nonpermanent contract of indefinite duration’ is temporary in nature and does not penalise abuse of temporary employment relationships. The Court recommends that these workers be given permanent status because they meet a structural and permanent need.

In the case of forest firefighters, this both infringes the workers’ rights and leaves our forests vulnerable – precisely when they are most at risk from fires as a result of drought and high temperatures – putting further strain on an already precarious sector. In view of this: 1.
How will the Commission ensure that the Spanish Government and the Autonomous Government of Valencia transpose Directive 1999/70/EC?

When will the Commission be able to ensure that Spain puts an end to its abuse of temporary government contracts, especially for forest firefighting teams, who are so crucial in the climate emergency?
answer: 1. Concerning the implementation of Directive 1999/70/EC (1), there are two ongoing infringements relating to the conformity of Spanish national legislation with the requirements of the framework Agreement annexed to that directive. One of them (INFR(2014)4334) relates to compliance with Clause 5 on abuse of successive fixed-term contracts. 2.

In the context of the Recovery and Resilience Plan (RRP), the Commission is also monitoring the completion of recruitment procedures to stabilise employment involving at least 300 000 posts (2), which will be assessed in the context of the seventh payment request, as set in the Council Implementing Decision.

In its communication on managing climate risks (3), the Commission urges Member States to improve governance structures and coordination for managing climate risks. The Commission also calls for ensuring that risk owners at the national level possess the necessary capabilities and resources to effectively manage climate risks.
